sunsetPlanner.title: Different moods by day and night
sunsetPlanner.note: Tha Phae Gate is open all day. Early morning is quiet with soft light, great for photos; after dark the square lights up and the Sunday Night Market comes alive.
sunsetPlanner.photoTip: 🌅 The gate faces east — side-light from 6–8 am is best for the wall and pigeons; the blue hour after sunset is the golden window for night shots.
sunsetPlanner.weatherTip: ☀️ March–May is hot; bring sun protection and water. June–Oct is rainy season with afternoon showers.

quickFactsDashboard.title: Tha Phae Gate · At a glance
quickFactsDashboard.intro: Everything you need to know about this Chiang Mai landmark at a glance.

items.label: Gate type
items.desc: One of the five main gates planned when King Mangrai walled the city in 1296; the present structure was rebuilt in the 1980s from historical records.

items.label: Founded
items.desc: Built with the moat and walls when King Mangrai (Mangrai) founded Chiang Mai; the current gate was rebuilt in 1985–1986.

items.label: District
items.desc: Midway along the eastern wall of the Old City; outside the gate is Tha Phae Road, leading east to the night bazaar and the Ping River.

items.label: Landmark type
items.desc: Both a historic monument and a civic gathering place, photo spot and festival venue.

items.label: Coordinates
items.desc: Plus Code: QXQV+48 Chiang Mai. Locatable directly on Google Maps.

items.label: Admission
items.desc: An open public square, no ticket, accessible any time; nearby temples charge separately.

hiddenRules.title: Tips for a comfortable visit
hiddenRules.subtitle: A few small habits make your Old City trip easier.

items.label: Shoes & dress
items.text: The square and old town are open-air; wear comfortable shoes. Cover shoulders and knees when entering nearby temples.

items.label: Weather & sun
items.text: Chiang Mai is sunny and hot by afternoon; bring a hat, sunscreen and water. June–Oct is rainy season — carry an umbrella.

items.label: Pigeons & photos
items.text: The square's pigeons are a popular photo subject; do not chase or feed them, and follow on-site municipal rules. Drones must follow local rules.

items.label: Courtesy & volume
items.text: This is a public square near temples; keep your voice down and respect the old walls.

items.label: Litter & cleanliness
items.text: Take your rubbish with you to protect the old town; sort waste, especially on market nights.

items.label: Safety & belongings
items.text: Crowds are dense — watch your phone and bag. It is safe at night, but stay aware.

complianceGuide.title: Visit respectfully · Protect the old city together
complianceGuide.subtitle: Tha Phae Gate is Chiang Mai's public space; a few simple manners help everyone enjoy it.

rules.title: Respect religious sites
rules.text: Nearby temples are places of worship — remove shoes, cover shoulders and knees, don't shout or climb on Buddha images.

rules.title: Animal protection & laws
rules.text: While the pigeon square is a photo hotspot, feeding pigeons is strictly prohibited by law (violators face heavy fines). Pigeon droppings are acidic and severely corrode the ancient red-brick walls. Please do not buy feed or feed them, helping protect both ecology and heritage.

rules.title: Heritage protection
rules.text: The ancient walls and gates are irreplaceable historical relics. Please do not climb, lean on, or vandalize the red brick walls. Maintain a respectful distance when taking photos and watch for warning signs.

rules.title: Be considerate
rules.text: Crowds at the square, crossings and night market are dense — yield to pedestrians, follow on-site guidance, and look after the elderly and children.

higashiyamaRoute.title: Recommended routes
higashiyamaRoute.subtitle: Two options: take the half-day route if you are short on time, or the full-day route to see the Old City properly.

plans.name: Half-day classic
plans.summary: Start at the gate and walk the eastern half of the Old City, covering the key temples and streets at a relaxed pace on mostly flat ground.
plans.tip: From Sunday afternoon Tha Phae Road becomes a pedestrian street and gets much busier — do the main stretch in the morning if you can.

plans.name: Full-day in depth
plans.bestTime: Start at 7:00 am, return to the gate around sunset for the lights
plans.summary: Extends the half-day route west into the very heart of the Old City, adding museums, a market and a cluster of temples — ideal if you like to take your time.

steps.title: Tha Phae Gate square
steps.text: First orient yourself at the gate facade and the information boards: outside lies Tha Phae Road toward the Ping River, inside the main east–west axis of the Old City.
tips: Morning light is softest — photograph the gate front before heading in.

steps.title: North along the east wall and moat
steps.text: Head north beside the wall and moat and look at how gate, corner bastions and water formed a single defensive system. The moat also supports aquatic plants and city birds.
tips: There is a walkway along the moat; the roadside trees give the best shade in the hot season.

steps.title: Three Kings Monument · City Arts & Cultural Centre
steps.text: The bronze monument to the three founding kings (Mangrai, Ramkhamhaeng and Ngam Muang) stands at the geographic centre of the Old City; the neighbouring arts centre gives a quick overview of Lanna history.
tips: The square in front is the easiest meeting point inside the Old City.

steps.title: Wat Phra Singh
steps.text: One of the most important Lanna temples in Chiang Mai, known for the Phra Singh Buddha and an exquisite Lanna-style scripture library; the murals and architectural detail reward a slow look.
tips: Remove shoes before entering halls, cover shoulders and knees, and never pose with your back to a Buddha image.

steps.title: Wat Chedi Luang · Wat Phan Tao
steps.text: The enormous ruined stupa of Wat Chedi Luang is one of Chiang Mai's most striking monuments; next door, Wat Phan Tao is famed for its all-teak hall. Visit both together.
tips: Temples usually stop admitting visitors around 5:00 pm, so schedule this for the earlier afternoon.

steps.title: Somphet Market · lunch and rest
steps.text: A traditional market on the north-east side of the Old City, strong on fresh produce, spices and cooked food — a good place for a northern Thai lunch and to restock water and fruit.
tips: 1:00–3:00 pm is the hottest window of the year; a perfect time to sit down and cool off.

steps.title: Wat Lok Moli · northern stretch of the wall
steps.text: Walk the northern stretch of the wall and moat and detour to Wat Lok Moli, known for its wooden structures and teak carving. This section is noticeably quieter than the temple core.
tips: A good stretch to slow down and look at how the wall meets the moat.

steps.title: Back to Tha Phae Gate · lights and night market
steps.text: Return around sunset, when the square lights come on — the golden window for photography. On Sundays Tha Phae Road is already a pedestrian street, so you can finish with the night market.
tips: The Sunday market starts after 4:00 pm; plan your trip home via the inner Old City roads.

plans.tip: The full-day route covers a lot of ground: wear soft-soled shoes and carry water. If energy is limited, take a red songthaew for the 'Wat Lok Moli · northern wall' section.

steps.title: Tha Phae Gate square
steps.text: Begin at the gate and pigeon square; morning light is softest. Read the info boards to understand the old city layout, then head inside the walls.

steps.title: North along the east wall
steps.text: Follow the moat and wall northward to feel the square plan of the Lanna old city and its water system.

steps.title: Three Kings Monument
steps.text: A bronze monument to the three founding kings (Mangrai, Ramkhamhaeng, Ngam Muang) — the geographic heart of the old town and the best meeting point.

steps.title: Wat Chedi Luang & Wat Phra Singh
steps.text: Two of Chiang Mai's most important Lanna temples; see the giant ruined stupa, the scripture library and Lanna murals.

steps.title: Back to Tha Phae Rd · Sunday Market
steps.text: Return to the gate area in the evening; on Sundays, stroll the famous Sunday Walking Street for food and crafts.

higashiyamaRoute.disclaimer: These routes are walking references; actual time depends on how long you linger and on the weather. The Sunday Walking Street closes Ratchadamnoen Road (the street immediately west of the gate) from ~16:00 on Sundays — go early to avoid crowds.

intro.title: What is Tha Phae Gate?
intro.description: Tha Phae Gate (ประตูท่าแพ) sits on the eastern wall of Chiang Mai's Old City and is its most representative gate — today also the city's living room. 'Tha Phae' means 'raft pier' in Thai: the gate historically faced the Ping River, where teak rafts landed to trade. Today the gate is free and open all day; its square is a hub for photos, gatherings and festivals, and the starting point of the Sunday Walking Street.

officialManagement.title: Management & on-site services
officialManagement.text: The square is managed by the Chiang Mai City Municipality (เทศบาลนครเชียงใหม่) as public space — daily opening, maintenance and festival setup are coordinated by them; info boards and volunteers offer basic guidance. Nearby temples are managed by the monasteries and the Fine Arts Department.

alsoKnownAs.title: You may also hear it called
items: The 'East Gate' of Chiang Mai: one of the five main gates, the eastern link between the old city and the outside (night bazaar, Ping River).
Home of the living room and the pigeons: an open square with year-round pigeons, a favorite rest, photo and meeting spot for visitors and locals.

Start of the Sunday Walking Street: every Sunday evening, Ratchadamnoen Road — the street immediately west of the gate — closes from the gate into a pedestrian market — one of Chiang Mai's most famous events.

transportSection.title: Getting to Tha Phae Gate · Transport
transportSection.subtitle: The gate is on the east side of the Old City, about 7 km from Chiang Mai International Airport; walking, red songthaew and Grab are all easy within the old town.
transportSection.overviewText: Tha Phae Gate is among the easiest Chiang Mai landmarks to reach: a 15–20 min taxi from the airport; the old town is compact and most sights are walkable.
transportSection.overviewText2: The gate itself is an open square with no ticket booth or fence; the Tha Phae Road / Old City Road junction nearby is the old town's transport hub.
arrivalItems: From Chiang Mai International (CNX) by taxi or Grab straight to the east gate.
Within the old town, hop on a red songthaew — wave to stop, hop on and off.
Stay near the old town or night bazaar and walk to most temples and markets.

modes.label: Flight + transfer
modes.title: Airport to old town
modes.description: Chiang Mai International is about 7 km from the gate — the entry point for most international and domestic travelers.
details: Airport shuttle / Grab / taxi reach the east gate in about 15–20 minutes.
Late-night arrivals are easy too; the gate area is reachable 24 hours.

steps.t: Use Grab or the airport taxi counter after arrivals.
Get off and walk into the square; signs are posted along the way.

modes.label: Songthaew
modes.title: Red Songthaew
modes.description: The most convenient transport in and around the old town, priced by distance, great for short hops.
details: Wave to stop and tell the driver 'Tha Phae Gate'.
Handy for the old town, night market and nearby temples.

modes.label: Grab / taxi
modes.title: Ride-hailing
modes.description: Book a Grab straight to the gate — transparent pricing and accurate location.
details: Easy from the night market, riverside or your hotel.
Book a bit earlier during peak (night-market evenings).

modes.label: Walk / bike
modes.title: Slow travel
modes.description: The old town is compact; from the gate most temples and markets are walkable.
details: Bike rental is available in the old town; riding the moat path is pleasant.
On Sunday market nights Tha Phae Road is pedestrian-only — walking is best.

parking.title: Parking info
parking.note: The gate is an open square with no dedicated parking; drivers can use nearby commercial lots and walk in.

options.name: Commercial lots along Tha Phae Rd

parking.disclaimer: Prices are estimates — follow on-site signs. During festivals and market nights spaces are tight; arrive early or use transit.

localTips: Early morning and late afternoon have the fewest crowds and the best light for photos.
Cafés, convenience stores and ATMs around the square make resupply easy.
On Sunday market nights, use the gate as your start and walk west along the street.

bestTime.title: Best time to visit
bestTime.text: For photos choose 6–9 am; for festivals and market atmosphere, Sunday evening to night. Open all day, no booking needed.

humanities.title: The culture beyond the gate
humanities.subtitle: Tha Phae Gate is more than a gate — it is a key to understanding the Lanna old city.

sections.title: 1296 · Founding of Lanna & the walls
sections.content: King Mangrai founded Chiang Mai in 1296 and built the moat and walls. Tha Phae Gate was originally known as 'Chiang Rueak Gate'. 'Tha Phae' means 'raft pier', reflecting its historical role as a water trade hub connecting to the Ping River. It served as the main eastern entrance to the Old City.

cards.title: King Mangrai
cards.text: Founder of the Lanna kingdom, who planned Chiang Mai's square city and moat system.

cards.title: Moat & walls
cards.text: The square moat (คูเมือง) and earthen-stone walls formed the city's defensive core.

cards.title: Five main gates
cards.text: The old city had east, west, south, north gates; Tha Phae was the eastern portal.

sections.title: 16th–18th c. · War & change
sections.content: During the Burmese Toungoo occupation (from 1558), walls and gates saw repeated fighting and repair; as the capital's focus shifted, parts of the wall fell into ruin.

fieldNote.title: What to see
fieldNote.text: Remaining wall sections can still be traced along the moat path — tangible evidence of the city's changes.

sections.title: 1985–1986 · Reconstruction
sections.content: The current red-brick gate is not the original 1296 structure. In 1985, to prepare for Chiang Mai's 700th anniversary, the Fine Arts Department reconstructed the ruined gate based on old photographs and historical archives. This greatly enhanced its documentary and visual value as a historical landmark.

academicNote.title: On the dates
academicNote.text: The present gate is a late-20th-century reconstruction; the original walls are older, and exact rebuild years vary by source.

sections.title: Modern · Civic square & festival portal
sections.content: Tha Phae Gate is more than an ancient monument; it is Chiang Mai's 'living room'. It serves as the core stage for major public festivals: the main battleground of Songkran, the starting point of the Loy Krathong parade, and the portal to the famous Sunday Night Market.

sections.title: Belief · Lanna astrology & guardian spirits
sections.content: The eight gates of Chiang Mai's old city (including the corner bastions) closely correspond to Lanna astrology (Bagua). Each gate houses a specific guardian spirit. Tha Phae Gate is not only a physical defense but also a spiritual boundary, allowing visitors to feel the site's profound cultural significance.

sections.title: Festivals · Market & tradition
sections.content: During Songkran (Thai New Year water festival), Loy Krathong, Yi Peng (lantern festival) and the Flower Festival, the area around the gate hosts major celebrations; every Sunday is the famous Walking Street.

cards.title: Sunday Walking Street
cards.text: Every Sunday evening, a pedestrian market stretching west from the gate — a signature Chiang Mai experience.

cards.title: Songkran
cards.text: The Thai New Year water festival; the gate area is a core celebration zone of the old city.

cards.title: Loy Krathong / Yi Peng
cards.text: Season of floating krathongs and sky lanterns; the old city and moat glow with light.

sections.title: Imagery · Gate & old city
sections.content: 'Tha Phae' means raft pier, echoing the city's river-born history; the gate, moat and walls together form the complete experience of Chiang Mai's Old City.

didYouKnow.title: Did you know?
didYouKnow.text: The Thai 'ท่าแพ' literally means 'raft pier' — because the gate historically faced the Ping River, where teak rafts floated down to land and trade.

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.subtitle: Transport, history, visiting and surroundings — cleared up first.

items.q: Are there restrooms at the gate?
items.a: The square is open with no dedicated restroom; use nearby cafés, convenience stores and malls.

items.q: Can I drive to the gate? Is parking easy?
items.a: Vehicles cannot enter the square; park at nearby commercial lots and walk in. Spaces in the old town are limited — prefer transit.
The square and ground are flat with no steps; wheelchairs and strollers move easily, with good sidewalk and crossing connections.
Cafés and convenience stores along Tha Phae Road offer resupply, charging and rest.
Thai 'ท่าแพ' means raft pier — the gate historically faced the Ping River, where teak rafts landed to trade.
Chiang Mai was founded by King Mangrai in 1296 with walls; the present gate was rebuilt in the 1980s from records.

items.q: What is the gate's relation to the old city?
items.a: It is the eastern gate; outside is Tha Phae Road, leading east to the night bazaar and Ping River — the eastern portal of the old city.

items.q: Is there an entrance fee? What are the hours?
items.a: Free and open 24 hours; no booking. Nearby temples charge separately.

items.q: How long should I plan for?
items.a: A quick stop is 20–30 min; with a half-day old-city walk and Sunday market, plan half a day.

items.q: When is the best time to go?
items.a: Early morning has few crowds and good light for photos; Sunday evening to night has the Walking Street at its liveliest.

items.q: What else is a must nearby?
items.a: Wat Chedi Luang, Wat Phra Singh and the Three Kings Monument inside the old city, plus the night bazaar and Ping River east of Tha Phae Road.

items.q: How to enjoy the Sunday Market?
items.a: From ~16:00 every Sunday, Ratchadamnoen Road (immediately west of the gate) closes into a pedestrian street — start at the gate and head west.
The flat square and pigeon watching are family-friendly; just watch sun protection and hydration.

items.q: What are the GPS coordinates and Plus Code of Tha Phae Gate?
items.a: 18.7878, 98.9933 — Plus Code QXQV+48 Chiang Mai. Paste either into Google Maps or a ride-hailing app and it drops you at the gate; the square itself has no street number.

items.q: Can I walk the old city walls and moat from the gate?
items.a: Yes. The gate is the eastern entrance of the square moat and rampart circuit that still defines Chiang Mai Old City, with a walking lane beside the water and about 6.5 km around the full loop. The brickwork you see was rebuilt in the 1980s on the original footprint, so it is a reconstruction rather than 13th-century fabric.

items.q: Is this an officially managed heritage site?
items.a: The gate and the surrounding square are public space maintained by Chiang Mai Municipality: no ticket booth, no gatekeeper, open day and night. For national-level tourism information see the Tourism Authority of Thailand link in our sources.

items.q: How do I get here from Chiang Mai Airport, and what does it cost?
items.a: Chiang Mai International Airport (CNX) is about 7 km away. A metered taxi from the airport counter is roughly 150–200 THB and takes 15–20 minutes, Grab usually quotes 120–250 THB depending on demand, and a red songthaew inside the Old City costs about 30–50 THB per person.

items.q: How should I photograph the pigeons?
items.a: Shoot from outside the flock at a low angle instead of chasing or cornering the birds, and never handle them. Skip the feed if you only want a photo: concentrated feeding crowds the square, accelerates wear on the brickwork and creates hygiene problems. Early morning has the softest light and the fewest people.

bilingual.title: Tha Phae Gate in English
bilingual.subtitle: A bilingual Thai–English reference for guides, students and anyone searching for ประตูท่าแพ ภาษาอังกฤษ — Thai heading, English body text you can quote.
bilingual.note: These English paragraphs are written for non-commercial guiding and classroom use; please credit this site.

cards.thTitle: ประวัติและที่มาของชื่อ "ท่าแพ"
cards.en: "Tha Phae" combines thâa (landing, pier) and phae (raft): the name describes a raft landing on the riverbank, not the shape of the gate. King Mangrai founded the walled city in 1296, when the Ping River ran much closer to the east wall, so this gate faced the trading waterfront. The brick gate standing today was rebuilt in the 1980s on the original footprint, which is why the masonry looks far newer than the 13th-century foundation.

cards.thTitle: กำแพงเมืองและคูเมือง
cards.en: Tha Phae Gate is the eastern entrance of the square moat and rampart circuit that still defines Chiang Mai Old City — roughly 1.6 km per side, with a walking lane beside the water. The moat began as a defensive system and now drains storm water, cools the inner city, and shelters birds and aquatic plants, while the wall's brick and mortar suffers from salt efflorescence in the rainy season.

cards.thTitle: การเยี่ยมชมและมารยาท
cards.en: The square is free and open around the clock: no ticket booth, no closing time. Cover your shoulders and knees and remove your shoes before entering nearby temples, keep your voice low, do not climb or sit on the brickwork, and do not feed the pigeons — feeding concentrates the flock, accelerates corrosion of the monument and creates hygiene risks. On Sundays from about 16:00, Ratchadamnoen Road — the street immediately west of the gate — closes for the Walking Street market.

stops: Gate square (watch the pigeons and city wall)
Nearby convenience store for water and ice cream
Snack section of the Sunday market
items.tip: Strollers roll easily on the square. There is no shade in the open middle, so bring hats and water at midday and keep an eye on passing vehicles and bicycles.

items.resonance: The gate faces east, so mornings give side-light; the moat banks offer reliable waterbirds and vegetation, and the light is richest around sunset.
stops: Eastern side-light on the gate at dawn
Brick texture and the pigeon flock
items.tip: Bring wide-angle and mid-range lenses; on Sunday market nights it is crowded, so arrive early to hold a spot. Never climb the wall or feed birds for a shot.

items.pace: Very slow · turn back any time

stops: Stay near the square entrance for views and photos
Shaded rest points at shops and cafés
The gentler stretch of the moat-side walkway
Return to the nearest drop-off point
items.tip: Some sidewalks and crossings have kerbs or no ramps — cross where there are traffic lights and allow extra time. Going with a companion is recommended.

items.resonance: The gate, the walls and the on-site information boards together tell a condensed history of the Lanna founding — the best place to start understanding Chiang Mai's layout.
stops: Gate plaques and the gate's form
The defensive system along the east wall and moat
Three Kings Monument and the City Arts & Cultural Centre

items.tip: Read alongside the bilingual Thai–English plaques on site for deeper understanding; dress modestly and keep your voice down inside temples.

stops: Walk on to the main old-city temples
Finish at the Sunday market or a nearby restaurant

services.title: Visitor services & nearby facilities
services.subtitle: What kinds of public services you can normally find around the square, described by category so you can plan accordingly.
services.neutralNote: This is a non-profit information project. The notes below describe facility types neutrally; we do not recommend or rate any specific business and have no commercial partnerships. Distances and hours are estimated ranges from public information — always check current signage and prices on site.

items.name: Public toilets
items.where: Nearby malls, convenience stores and petrol stations
items.detail: There are no fixed public toilets on the gate square itself; the nearest are usually inside nearby malls, convenience stores or petrol stations. If you use a shop's facilities, buying something small is courteous.
items.tip: Carry tissues and small change — a small cleaning fee applies in some places.

items.name: Drinking water
items.where: Convenience stores, supermarkets and roadside stalls
items.detail: Bottled water is available everywhere from convenience stores and supermarkets; roadside drink stalls also cluster around the square. In the hot and rainy seasons humidity is high — aim to drink water every hour.
items.tip: Pick up an electrolyte drink at a convenience store to avoid afternoon heat exhaustion.

items.name: Parking
items.where: Outer ring road and shopping-centre car parks
items.detail: The gate sits on a main road, so kerbside spaces are limited and often restricted by time. If you drive, park on the outer ring road or in a nearby shopping-centre car park and walk in.
items.tip: On Sunday market nights Ratchadamnoen Road (west of the gate) closes and demand peaks — arrive early or use another mode of transport.

items.name: Fuel & EV charging
items.where: Main roads outside the Old City
items.detail: Petrol stations are mostly on the outer ring and the main roads leaving the city; EV chargers are concentrated in large mall and hotel car parks.
items.tip: Fill up before renting a car or scooter — there is no petrol station inside the Old City.

items.name: Dining (full meals)
items.where: Tha Phae Road, Old City lanes and market stalls
items.detail: The area covers everything from northern Thai home cooking and noodle shops to halal and vegetarian options; during market hours, street-food stalls dominate.
items.tip: Choose stalls that cook to order and turn tables quickly; if you have a sensitive stomach, avoid raw or long-standing cooked food.

items.name: Coffee & light bites
items.where: Along Tha Phae Road and in Old City lanes
items.detail: Chiang Mai has a strong coffee culture and cafés are dense within walking distance of the square — a good way to escape heat or rain mid-route.
items.tip: Indoor seats fill up fast during afternoon thunderstorms, so go in a little earlier.

items.name: Convenience stores & supermarkets
items.detail: Chain convenience stores cluster at the main intersections and keep long hours; larger supermarkets are in the shopping districts just outside the Old City.
items.tip: Useful for rain gear, sunscreen, mosquito repellent and basic medicine.

items.name: Accommodation
items.where: Inside the Old City, along Tha Phae Rd and the Ping River
items.detail: Options range from hostels and boutique guesthouses to business and resort hotels; most are within walking distance of the Old City core.
items.tip: Prices and crowds both rise during the Sunday market and festival periods — book ahead.

items.name: Cash & payments
items.where: Bank branches, malls and convenience stores
items.detail: ATMs are usually sited at bank branches, malls and convenience stores. Larger businesses generally accept cards and QR payments; night-market stalls mostly take cash or local QR codes.
items.tip: Keep a little cash for small purchases and cash-only stalls.

items.name: Medical care & pharmacies
items.where: Along the main roads inside and outside the Old City
items.detail: Pharmacies are spread along the main roads, and several general hospitals with emergency departments sit just outside the Old City.
items.tip: Emergency ambulance 1669; carrying your usual medication and a small first-aid kit is recommended.

items.name: Internet & connectivity
items.detail: Free Wi-Fi is standard in cafés, malls and hotels; local prepaid data SIMs can be bought at the airport, malls and convenience stores.
items.tip: Mobile data can slow noticeably at peak times — save important maps for offline use.

items.name: Accessibility
items.where: The square surface and main walkways
items.detail: The square is broadly level and step-free, so wheelchairs and strollers can get around; some sidewalks and crossings still have kerbs or lack ramps.
items.tip: Cross where there are traffic lights and allow extra time to get around.

items.name: Left luggage & lost property
items.where: Nearby shops and hotel front desks
items.detail: There is no official left-luggage point on the square, but some nearby shops and hotels will store bags; for lost items, ask the tourist police.
items.tip: Keep valuables on you and mind your bag while taking photos.

items.name: Help & safety
items.where: Tourist-police posts at main tourist-area junctions
items.detail: Tourist-police posts in the tourist areas can assist in several languages; in an emergency, call the national emergency numbers directly.

Rainy-season rainfall helps clear airborne particles, and the air is usually clearest then.

scienceDuty.title: Understanding & responsibility
scienceDuty.subtitle: Once you see why it matters, you know how to treat it.
scienceDuty.knowledgeTitle: A little building and ecology science

knowledge.title: Why old brick turns white
knowledge.body: In Chiang Mai's humid rainy season, soluble salts inside the brick migrate to the surface with moisture and crystallise into a white powder — efflorescence. It does not destroy the wall at once, but repeated cycles flake the brick face away, so limiting water contact and foot traffic helps slow the damage.

knowledge.title: Pigeons versus old buildings
knowledge.body: Pigeon droppings are acidic and, over time, corrode stone and mortar joints; dense flocks also create hygiene risks. The square's flock is largely a product of human feeding, so not feeding them is the simplest way to protect both the monument and your own health.

knowledge.title: The moat is not just scenery
knowledge.body: The moat began as part of the city's defences and also handled drainage and slope protection. Today it is a cooling water surface in the urban heat island and a habitat for birds. Its reeds and bank trees form a small urban ecological corridor.

knowledge.title: How the gate and wall were built
knowledge.body: Lanna gates are brick-and-stone arched structures, once topped by a wooden tower — what you see today is a reconstruction. The wall has a rammed-earth core faced with red brick, and its top is wide enough to walk, showing the three-layer 'city–wall–moat' defence design.

knowledge.title: Shade is a scarce resource
knowledge.body: The rain trees and banyans inside and outside the wall supply essential shade for the square and shelter for city birds. At midday in the hot season the perceived temperature under a tree can be several degrees lower, so please do not break branches, climb, or occupy tree pits.

knowledge.title: A reconstruction is not an original
knowledge.body: The gate you see today was rebuilt in the 1980s from historic photographs and documents, not the 13th-century original. Understanding the difference between a reconstruction and an original is the most basic — and most important — skill when visiting a heritage site.

scienceDuty.dutyIntro: Preserving a monument always costs more than repairing it. These six things are within every visitor's reach.

duty.title: Do not feed the pigeons
duty.body: Feeding concentrates the flock, speeds up corrosion of the monument and creates crowding and hygiene problems.

duty.title: Do not climb or lean on the wall
duty.body: Brick and mortar joints cannot take repeated loading — sitting or climbing for photos directly accelerates damage.

duty.title: Take your rubbish with you
duty.body: The square sees heavy evening footfall; put waste in the separated bins or carry it out.

duty.title: Keep the volume down
duty.body: The square borders homes and temples, so please avoid loudspeakers and prolonged shouting.

duty.title: Dress appropriately in temples
duty.body: Remove shoes and cover shoulders and knees before entering nearby temples; do not take selfies with your back to a Buddha image.

duty.title: Respect other people's image
duty.body: Ask before photographing passers-by, monks and vendors; commercial shoots require a permit.

scienceDuty.sourceNote: The notes above are general public-interest explanations. Where they differ from on-site plaques or official announcements, the on-site and official information takes precedence.

legends.title: History, legends & evidence
legends.subtitle: The gate's real name, the origin of the raft pier, and the stories Chiang Mai keeps telling.

stories.title: 'Tha Phae' was actually a pier
stories.subtitle: A commercial history hidden in the name
paragraphs: 'Tha Phae (ท่าแพ)' is made of two Thai words: Tha, meaning a landing or pier, and Phae, meaning raft. Together they simply mean 'raft pier'. The name tells you that this gate originally faced a busy riverbank, not an open square.

Historically the Ping River ran closer to the city wall than it does today. Teak and goods drifted downstream, landed outside the city, and entered the market through this gate. The gate was named for its function, not its shape or direction.
The riverbank now lies several hundred metres away, but the name stayed — a useful clue to the direction in which Chiang Mai grew.
stories.evidence: Toponymic evidence; the historic relationship between the eastern wall and the Ping River can be checked against old city maps and local records.

stories.title: The gate's real name was 'Chiang Rueak' — and an outer gate has vanished
stories.subtitle: The second gate that disappeared
paragraphs: In Lanna documents and local memory this gate is often called Pratu Chiang Rueak (ประตูเชียงเรือก), while the name Tha Phae belonged more to the pier market outside it.

The eastern side of the old city was never a single doorway: beyond the main gate stood an outer gate (ประตูหน้า), forming a double defence and a check point. When the walls lost their defensive role in the modern era, the outer gate was demolished along with most of the wall.
What you see today is therefore a reconstruction at the site of the inner gate; the outer gate and pier market that made this area thrive survive only in place names and street alignments.
stories.evidence: Differences in gate names between Lanna sources and local records; the existing reconstruction was based on late-19th to early-20th-century photographs.

stories.title: The founding legend: King Mangrai, a white elephant and Doi Suthep
stories.subtitle: Why the city was sited here
paragraphs: Tradition holds that in the late 13th century King Mangrai, the Lanna ruler, released a white elephant to determine the site and boundary of his new city — where the elephant settled was taken as auspicious ground. Chiang Mai ended up on the Ping plain, backed by Doi Suthep, giving the 'mountain–city–river' arrangement.

Another strand of the tradition stresses an alliance of three kings: Mangrai of Lanna, Ramkhamhaeng of Sukhothai and Ngam Muang of Phayao planned the city together — which is why the Three Kings Monument stands at its centre today.
The legend is not literal history, but it preserves something true: the site was chosen with water supply, flood control and defence in mind, a real feat of early urban planning.
stories.evidence: Northern Thai foundation legends and chronicle-style sources; archaeological and topographic research support the flood-control + water + defence logic.

stories.title: Gates and cardinal directions: Lanna astrology
stories.subtitle: Gates were more than entrances
paragraphs: Lanna urban planning was strongly shaped by astrological and directional ideas: the number of gates, their orientation and their guardian spirits carried symbolic meaning, so gates were boundaries of a city's cosmology as much as passageways.

The square wall and moat together defined 'inside' and 'outside', with gates as the nodes for movement and ritual. Most gates decayed through long use, and today only some positions have been restored.
For visitors, remembering the structure — square wall + moat + gates — is enough to find your bearings almost anywhere in the Old City.
stories.evidence: Studies of Lanna urban form and directional symbolism; surviving wall and moat alignments still match the traditional layout.

stories.title: A gate brought back from old photographs
stories.subtitle: The 1980s reconstruction
paragraphs: Photographs from the late 19th century show the gate already badly decayed, and parts of the wall had been removed for roads and civic works. For a long period this spot was simply a junction without a gateway.

In the 1980s, ahead of Chiang Mai's 700th anniversary, local authorities rebuilt the gate on its original alignment using historic photographs and documents, cleared and planted the surroundings, and created today's square.
That explains why the brickwork looks far newer than something from the 13th century: it is not an original, but an evidence-based reconstruction.
stories.evidence: Photographic archives from the late 19th century onward; the reconstruction dates to the 1980s and is linked to the city's 700th anniversary.

stories.title: How the square became a 'pigeon square'
stories.subtitle: A page of contemporary urban culture
paragraphs: After the gate was rebuilt the area became an open square, and feeding pigeons and taking photos gradually became a fixture for visitors. The flock grew, and travel guides began calling the place the 'pigeon square'.

In recent years environmental and heritage voices have urged visitors not to feed the birds, to ease the pressure on both the monument and public health — a familiar cycle of a destination becoming popular first and being managed afterwards.
Today the square also hosts festivals, parades, markets and everyday leisure, which makes it a good window onto how public space in Chiang Mai is actually used.
stories.evidence: Local media coverage and public statements relating to municipal cleaning and monument maintenance; the square's functions continue to shift with tourism and city management.
